{{Short description|Statistical test}}
The '''Sargan–Hansen test''' or '''Sargan's <math>J</math> test''' is a [[statistical test]] used for testing [[over-identifying restriction]]s in a [[statistical model]]. It was proposed by [[John Denis Sargan]] in 1958,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sargan |first=J. D. |year=1958 |title=The Estimation of Economic Relationships Using Instrumental Variables |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=393–415 |jstor=1907619 |doi=10.2307/1907619}}</ref> and several variants were derived by him in 1975.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sargan |first=J. D. |orig-year=1975 |year=1988 |chapter=Testing for misspecification after estimating using instrumental variables |title=Contributions to Econometrics |location=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-32570-6 }}</ref> [[Lars Peter Hansen]] re-worked through the derivations and showed that it can be extended to general non-linear [[Generalized method of moments|GMM]] in a [[time series]] context.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hansen |first=Lars Peter |year=1982 |title=Large Sample Properties of Generalized Method of Moments Estimators |journal=Econometrica |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=1029–1054 |jstor=1912775 |doi=10.2307/1912775}}</ref>

The Sargan test is based on the assumption that model parameters are identified via a priori restrictions on the coefficients, and tests the validity of over-identifying restrictions. The test statistic can be computed from [[Errors and residuals|residuals]] from [[instrumental variable]]s regression by constructing a quadratic form based on the cross-product of the residuals and exogenous variables.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sargan |first=J. D. |year=1988 |title=Lectures on Advanced Econometric Theory |location=Oxford |publisher=Basil Blackwell |isbn=0-631-14956-2 }}</ref>{{rp|132–33}} Under the null hypothesis that the over-identifying restrictions are valid, the statistic is asymptotically distributed as a [[Chi-squared distribution|chi-square]] variable with <math>(m - k)</math> degrees of freedom (where <math>m</math> is the number of instruments and <math>k</math> is the number of endogenous variables).
